the cardiometabolic risk is high in people with MetS or impaired glucose tolerance and in peri- and post-menopausal women with or without MetS, and that the risk is due to the presence of multiple inflammatory mediators and HDL dysfunction.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of inflammation and HDL dysfunction in the development and progression of cardiovascular disease in people with MetS and/or impaired glucose tolerance.
the cardiometabolic risk associated with MetS and its related conditions in the population at-large.
the role of inflammation and oxidative stress in cardiometabolic risk, especially in the presence of HDL dysfunction, which we believe is a common denominator in this risk.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the MetS and its associated risk factors, such as hypertriglyceridea, are associated with a pro-inflammatory state and a dysfunctional HDL, which are both important risk markers for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
HDL dysfunction is the main underlying mechanism of cardiometabolic risk, and that this dysfunction can be reversed by lifestyle modifications and/or pharmacotherapy.
apoA-I dysfunction is the most common and most important risk factor for cardiovascular disease and diabetes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HDL dysfunction, as a result of the pro-inflammatory state in MetS, is a common and major contributor to cardiometabolic risk.
apoA-I dysfunction is the main culprit for cardiometabolic risk, and that the best management of this risk is to prevent obesity and to improve the quality of life.
the MetS and its associated dyslipidemias are atherogenic and pro-inflammatory, and that apoA-I dysfunction is a key factor underlying the cardiometabolic risk of the MetS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the MetS and impaired glucose tolerance are not benign conditions.
HDL dysfunction and apoA-I deficiency are common in the population at-large, and that they are associated with atherogenic dysmetabolism and cardiometabolic risk.
HDL function is an important determinant of cardiometabolic risk.
